# Every coupling with uniform endpoint marginals can give an insufficient target

This exact example rules out another auxiliary transport mechanism. It
does not refute (OC): the target measures considered below are particular
transported measures on the middle fiber, not the original mixed measure.

## Statement

There is a full-dimensional convex body \(C\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\)
with three positive-area integer fibers \(K_-,T,K_+\), whose unique
weighted median integer index is zero, such that the following holds.
For **every** coupling of uniform random points \(X\in K_-\), \(Y\in K_+\),
the middle-fiber target
\[
 \eta=1_T\,\mathcal L^2+min(|K_-|,|K_+|)
                  \operatorname{Law}((X+Y)/2)
\]
has maximum unnormalized halfspace depth strictly smaller than
\(\gamma_2\mu(C\cap(\mathbb Z\times\mathbb R^2))/2\).
Independence is unnecessary for this obstruction. Couplings with
singular laws and boundary atoms are included.

## Exact body and parameters

Put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\},\\
 A=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(4/5,0),(0,8/25)\},\\
 \epsilon=2^{-20},\qquad s=3/128+\epsilon,\\
 K_-=(2-s)A,\qquad K_+=sA,\\
 C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((\{-1\}\times K_-)
        \cup(\{0\}\times T)\cup(\{1\}\times K_+)\bigr).
 \end{gathered}
\]
The endpoint fibers are exact, and the middle fiber is exact because
\((K_-+K_+)/2=A\subset T\). There are no further integer indices.
The body has nonempty interior in \(\mathbb R^3\), and all three fibers
have positive area. Thus the relevant Hausdorff measure is ordinary
two-dimensional area summed over the fibers.

Write \(c=|T|=1/2\), \(a=|K_-|\), \(b=|K_+|\), and \(M=a+b+c\).
With
\[
 e=\frac{32}{125}s^2=\frac{604028929}{4294967296000},
 \qquad \delta=\frac{128}{125}\epsilon,
\]
the exact volume relations are
\[
 b/c=e,\qquad a/c=1+e-\delta,
 \qquad M/c=2+2e-\delta. \tag{1}
\]
In particular \(a> b\), so the paired mass is \(b\). Both strict-side
masses at index zero are less than \(M/2\). At index \(-1\) the opposite
mass \(b+c\) exceeds \(M/2\), because \(a<b+c\); at index \(1\) the
opposite mass \(a+c\) exceeds \(M/2\). Thus zero is the unique weighted
median integer index. In fact each of the three fibers has mass less
than \(M/2\), since also \(2e>\delta\).

The desired original OC mass, divided by \(c\), is
\[
 \tau=\frac{2M}{9c}=\frac29(2+2e-\delta). \tag{2}
\]

## A uniform tail estimate valid for every coupling

For an arbitrary coupling of the two endpoint uniform laws, write
\[
 X=(2-s)U,\qquad Y=sV,
\]
where each of \(U,V\) is uniform on \(A\), with their joint law unrestricted.
Their midpoint is
\[
 Z=\alpha U+\beta V,
 \qquad \alpha=1-s/2,\quad \beta=s/2,\quad\alpha+\beta=1.
\]
For uniform \(U\in A\), the exact tails needed below are
\[
 \Pr\!\left(\frac{U_x}{4/5}\ge t\right)=(1-t)^2
       \quad (0\le t\le1), \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
 \Pr\!\left(\frac{U_x+U_y}{4/5}>t\right)
       =\frac{(1-t)^2}{3/5}
       \quad (2/5\le t\le1). \tag{4}
\]
For (3), the retained cap is a similar triangle with linear scale
\(1-t\). For (4), the linear functional \((x+y)/(4/5)\) takes values
\(0,1,2/5\) at the three vertices. Above the middle vertex value, the cap
at the value-one vertex has edge fractions \(1-t\) and
\((1-t)/(1-2/5)\); their product gives the displayed area fraction.
Strict and weak inequalities give the same probabilities in (3)-(4),
because the uniform marginal is absolutely continuous.

Define rational thresholds
\[
 a_0=\frac13-\frac{e}{16},\qquad
 b_0=\frac13-\frac{41e}{125},\qquad
 u=\frac54a_0,\qquad v=\frac54(a_0+b_0).
\]
The exact parameters satisfy
\[
 \beta<u<1,\qquad \frac25<\frac v\alpha<1,
 \qquad\frac8{25}<b_0<1,
 \qquad0<a_0<a_0+b_0<1. \tag{5}
\]
All these rational comparisons are verified by the companion script.
They can also be checked directly from
\(9/64000<e<1/6250\) and \(3/128<s<1/40\).

Since \(V_x/(4/5)\le1\), the event \(Z_x\ge a_0\) implies
\[
 U_x/(4/5)\ge (u-\beta)/\alpha.
\]
By (3) and (5), every coupling therefore satisfies
\[
 \Pr(Z_x\ge a_0)\le\left(\frac{1-u}{\alpha}\right)^2. \tag{6}
\]
Since \(U_y,V_y\le8/25\), equation (5) gives
\[
 \Pr(Z_y\ge b_0)=0. \tag{7}
\]
Finally \(V_x+V_y\ge0\), so the strict event
\((U_x+U_y)/(4/5)>v/\alpha\) implies
\(Z_x+Z_y>a_0+b_0\). Equations (4)-(5) yield
\[
 \Pr(Z_x+Z_y\le a_0+b_0)
 \le1-\frac{((\alpha-v)/\alpha)^2}{3/5}. \tag{8}
\]
The strict implication used here is why (8) remains valid even if the
coupling makes the law of \(Z\) charge the boundary of the closed cap.
No regularity of the joint law was used.

## Three fixed caps cover every possible target center

Consider the following closed halfplanes of the continuous plane:
\[
 H_1=\{x\ge a_0\},\qquad H_2=\{y\ge b_0\},
 \qquad H_3=\{x+y\le a_0+b_0\}.
\]
They cover all of \(\mathbb R^2\): outside the first two, both strict
reverse inequalities hold, which implies membership in the third.
Thus they cover every possible point of the middle fiber, including all
their boundaries.

For \(\eta=1_T\mathcal L^2+b\operatorname{Law}(Z)\), the cap masses
divided by \(c\) are bounded, respectively, by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 U_1&=(1-a_0)^2+e\left(\frac{1-u}{\alpha}\right)^2,\\
 U_2&=(1-b_0)^2,\\
 U_3&=(a_0+b_0)^2
            +e\left[1-\frac{((\alpha-v)/\alpha)^2}{3/5}\right].
 \end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Here the terms from \(T\) are its elementary similar-triangle cap areas;
the paired terms follow from (6)-(8).

Substitution of the rational parameters into (2) and (9) gives the exact
positive differences
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau-U_1&=
 \frac{1432514278136662974050522862997520267}
 {912835900916101579792855125196800000000000},\\
 \tau-U_2&=
 \frac{2025814712493388791956711}
 {2594073385365405696000000000000},\\
 \tau-U_3&=
 \frac{5478570717192890979361486970803017356213}
 {8557836571088452310558016798720000000000000000}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Each exceeds \(6/10^7\), as direct cross multiplication verifies.
These are exact identities; no numerical optimization or approximate
integration enters the argument.

For every candidate point \(w\in\mathbb R^2\), at least one of the three
closed halfplanes contains it, and (9)-(10) bound that halfplane's target
mass strictly below \(c\tau=2M/9\). Consequently
\[
 \sup_{w\in\mathbb R^2}\inf_{H\ni w}\eta(H)
 \le c\max(U_1,U_2,U_3)<\frac29M.
\]
This is stronger than failure of a log-concavity or radial-convexity
property: the required target depth itself fails, for every coupling
with the specified uniform endpoint marginals.

## Scope

The construction does not exclude selecting a nonuniform submeasure of
the larger endpoint, changing the singleton allocation, using several
transport targets, or proving (OC) directly. In particular, it is not a
counterexample to the original mixed-integer statement. It shows that
arbitrary dependence cannot repair the strategy that retains the full
middle measure and pairs the two uniformly normalized endpoint laws
with their entire smaller mass.
